section.title: Modularity makes correctness a problem you can reason about
section.deck: Barbara Liskov traces data abstraction and distributed systems through practical problems, research freedom, and ideas that became invisible through success.

blocks.question: How did you enter programming when graduate education could exclude women?
answer: After completing an undergraduate mathematics degree, Liskov applied to graduate programs. Princeton sent a postcard saying it did not admit women. She had known about its undergraduate restriction but had not realized the graduate program was also closed to her. Berkeley did admit her, but she decided she was not ready for a mathematics PhD and wanted to work first. The best job offer was programming, which she calls a fortunate accident that brought her into computer science.

The host notes that she had been a strong student and still faced a closed door. Liskov contrasts that institutional exclusion with Berkeley’s environment: her mathematics classes had few women, but the university did not treat the subject as something women were prohibited from doing. She separates low representation from an explicit denial of access rather than turning the story into one undifferentiated description of every institution.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: What was the software crisis, and what made large programs fail?
answer: Liskov recalls reports of organizations spending large sums and hundreds of person-years on systems they ultimately discarded because the programs did not work. The missing discipline was modular design: divide the system into components whose interfaces explain the service they provide, while hiding their implementations.

With an appropriate decomposition, correctness can be reasoned about one module at a time. But procedures were the main mechanism offered by languages of that era, and a procedure did not naturally represent a stateful service such as a filesystem or a database. The problem was not simply how to cut a large file into smaller files. It was finding a module concept that matched the design of a real system.

followups.question: What were the early proposed solutions, and how did you find data abstraction?
answer: Researchers talked about modularity without a clear account of what a module was. Some treated a module as a chunk of code of a particular size, which Liskov did not consider a sufficient design rule.

Earlier work at Mitre had given her a more complete mechanism. A small team was building a complicated system, and she wanted to keep the programmers from interfering with each other. A component exposed a collection of operations while its internal data remained inaccessible. She eventually recognized that this could represent a set, sequence, or other abstract data type. In hindsight, she saw related papers as close to the idea: it was a moment when several pieces were ready to fit together.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: How did this work in CLU influence programming languages beyond the research project?
answer: Liskov and Steve Zilles wrote a paper outlining abstract data types and how a language could support them. It had an immediate effect in the research community, and CLU then developed the language-level ideas further.

She chose not to turn CLU into a commercial product. She preferred research, and companies of that period generally wanted an organization standing behind a language rather than downloading an independently shared project. CLU still had users, but broad adoption also came through later languages. She identifies Ada as a prominent language designed with data abstraction and Java as another later step in the influence of the underlying ideas.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: What concerned you about Python’s modules?
answer: Liskov’s criticism is about encapsulation: code outside a module can interfere with its internal state. She regards protection of that boundary as essential to modularity, especially when many programmers work on a large system. Compiler-enforced restrictions can prevent a weak implementation or misuse from undermining the whole team. She also acknowledges that Python serves other goals and says she no longer considers herself a programming-language expert. The argument is her view of the tradeoff, not a comprehensive evaluation of Python’s current ecosystem.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: What drew you into distributed computing?
answer: A paper by Bob Kahn described programs composed of pieces on different networked computers, at a time when how to build those systems was still unclear. Liskov saw an important open problem while looking for a new direction. Her first project was a language for distributed programs; subsequent work followed the problems that project exposed.

followups.question: What was that language, and how did it manage a computation spanning machines?
answer: Argus was influenced by CLU. A guardian was a module on one machine, and guardians communicated with remote procedure calls. A computation using several guardians needed to complete as a whole or leave no effect. Liskov borrowed transactions from databases so those computations could run atomically. That work led toward storing replicated data with correct behavior and availability when enough nodes and the network remained operational.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

followups.question: What does a viewstamp represent?
answer: It lets the system identify sufficiently recent state when a node fails and another must take over. The goal is to continue without losing already completed work. The clip gives the intuition rather than a full protocol specification.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

followups.question: What happens when clocks disagree?
answer: The mechanism does not depend on synchronized wall clocks. Liskov says the views are numbered: one view is followed by the next numbered view. The host recognizes this as passing and incrementing logical numbers rather than comparing clock readings.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: Did you develop this work together with Leslie Lamport?
answer: No. Liskov says they independently reached essentially the same underlying idea: her Viewstamped Replication and Lamport’s Paxos. She is describing a shared core rather than claiming every presentation and implementation is identical.

followups.question: Are there significant advantages and disadvantages between the two approaches?
answer: She says there are technical details one can vary, but regards the main mechanism as substantially the same. She recalls a former student recognizing Viewstamped Replication in Google’s filesystem-related work while the people using it described it as Paxos. This is her account of recognizing the common idea.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: How did parallel work on object-oriented languages lead to the substitution principle?
answer: Liskov describes simultaneous but partly separate research streams: CLU, Smalltalk, and Alphard. When preparing an OOPSLA keynote, she read work based on Smalltalk and noticed an unresolved connection between implementation inheritance and type hierarchy.

Her own teaching with John Guttag emphasized module specifications, abstract data types, and correctness. It began with what a component meant; its implementation remained hidden. By contrast, some class descriptions she read explained how an implementation differed from its superclass. Thinking in terms of behavior gave her a way to state the required relation: a subclass used where a superclass is expected should behave appropriately for that context.

That insight became associated with the Liskov substitution principle. Liskov says her later paper with Jeannette Wing formalized behavioral subtyping. The interview’s account emphasizes expectations and meaning rather than treating reuse of a superclass implementation as sufficient proof of substitutability.

followups.question: Did you give the principle your own name?
answer: No. She discovered the name when someone emailed her in the 1990s asking whether an interpretation of the “Liskov substitution principle” was correct. By then she was working on other topics and had not been thinking about the idea’s growing visibility.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: Why do some names and ideas become better known than similar work?
answer: Asked why Paxos became more familiar than Viewstamped Replication, Liskov recalls Lamport’s explanation that he gave the talks while she implemented the work. She acknowledges his presentations and papers as a source of visibility. When the host wonders whether the catchier name also helped, she agrees that it is a appealing name without treating naming as a proven causal explanation.

She also reconnects the technical history to transactions: an ordinary transaction leader can become a serious problem if it fails, whereas the replication protocols had to move to a new leader safely. That change was the important advance she and Lamport reached independently.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.text: The conversation then distinguishes crash failures from nodes that act maliciously while appearing healthy. Liskov describes work with Brian Oki on Viewstamped Replication and later work with Miguel Castro on Byzantine-fault protocols, prompted by interest in attacks on networked systems. The captions mislabel one protocol in this passage; the discussion’s contrast between crash handling and Byzantine behavior is retained without assigning the inconsistent label to Castro’s work.
blocks.heading: A new failure model requires a new protocol

blocks.question: Did you meet Dijkstra, and what mattered about his argument against goto?
answer: Liskov met him several times but did not work with him. She notes that the famous goto text was a letter to the editor, and regards its importance as a statement about reasoning: correctness was not trivial just because someone could write code. At a time when computer science was dismissed as simple programming, that was a substantive argument for taking the discipline seriously.

followups.question: Why was the argument controversial?
answer: Some people needed goto because their languages, including assembly, lacked the structured constructs familiar today. Others worried that less direct control would produce inefficient code because compilers were weaker. Skilled programmers could also feel personally criticized. Liskov adds that Dijkstra’s manner was not especially diplomatic. The controversy involved practical limitations as well as offense; later languages and compilers changed the context.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

followups.question: Was he as blunt in person as in his writing?
answer: She says he was not always as tactful as he could have been, while also acknowledging his distinction as a researcher.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: Why stay in academia rather than move permanently into industry?
answer: Liskov enjoyed research and working with students. Although teaching was not her favorite part, she saw it as closely tied to research. She also points out that the boundary between professors and startups was different when she was young; founding a company alongside academic work was not the default path she saw.

She briefly worked in a startup in the late 1990s and preferred research. Academic freedom let her follow the zigzags visible across her career. She calls that freedom both a gift and a curse: it allows a researcher to choose a direction, but also makes deciding what is worth doing their responsibility.

followups.question: What keeps a researcher from pursuing a useless direction?
answer: Her blunt answer is that a researcher may not receive tenure. The freedom to choose a problem still operates within evaluation by a research community.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

followups.question: Who judges the value of that work?
answer: The research community is important. A research university cares substantially about how its faculty members are regarded by others in their field.
followups.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: Why are teaching and research so closely connected?
answer: Teaching from first principles demands a deep understanding of what works, what fails, and which assumptions are being made. Liskov sees good research as requiring the same reasoning process. Explaining a foundation and investigating it are therefore closely related intellectual work.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.text: When the host emphasizes choosing the right research direction, Liskov advises graduate students not to remain in a pattern of tiny incremental improvements. The goal is a good problem that admits a plausible solution and matches the researcher’s skills. Recognizing when a direction is productive—or is not—is part of the work, not something guaranteed by effort alone.
blocks.heading: Find a good problem, not just more work on the same one

blocks.question: What role did luck and setbacks play in your career?
answer: Liskov sees both luck and hard work. After her PhD, she wanted a faculty job but did not receive a good offer. Returning to Mitre gave her several years to change direction from AI toward systems without simultaneously taking on teaching and student responsibilities. A disappointment became a useful period of transition.

She also connects later academic opportunity with institutions opening more broadly to women. The recurring image is a set of doors: some close, another opens, and the person must decide whether to step through. She does not claim every setback is beneficial; she describes continuing to work through the available choices rather than letting one rejection halt her career.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov

blocks.question: Why did some people question the significance of your Turing Award work?
answer: Liskov first challenges the host’s assumption that only she faced negative comments. Her husband happened to read those comments online; she thinks other recipients may have encountered similar treatment if they looked.

Her more interesting interpretation is that some of the work had become so fundamental that people could no longer imagine the previous world. Even her graduate students had not fully grasped that abstract data types and the modular-programming mindset had to be invented. A specific protocol is easy to identify as an invention; a way of thinking that permeates ordinary practice can become part of the unnoticed background.

She therefore viewed the dismissive comments, despite their intent, as a kind of compliment to the broader research community that created those foundations. The impact had become difficult to see precisely because the ideas were taken for granted.
blocks.speaker: Barbara Liskov
